options.text: Adding `'use strict'` as the first line of `f` still makes `f.call(5)` return an object
options.why: In strict mode `this` is passed as is, so `f.call(5)` returns the number 5.

explanation: Sloppy-mode functions coerce `this`: null and undefined become the global object, and primitives are boxed. Strict functions skip this coercion. That is one reason strict mode is safer and faster: a strict method can receive a primitive `this` without allocating a wrapper.

stem: Which three statements about the `arguments` object are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: In strict mode, assigning to a parameter does not change `arguments[0]`, and vice versa
options.why: Strict functions always get an unmapped arguments object.

options.text: A sloppy-mode function with a default, rest or destructured parameter gets an unmapped `arguments` object
options.why: A non-simple parameter list switches off the mapping in sloppy mode too.

options.text: `arguments` is array-like: it has `length` and indexes but no array methods such as `map`
options.why: Convert it with `Array.from(arguments)` or use rest parameters instead.

options.text: Arrow functions get their own `arguments` object when they are called with arguments
options.why: Arrows never have their own `arguments`; the name refers to the enclosing function's object.
`arguments.length` is how many arguments were passed; `fn.length` is how many parameters were declared.
Reading `arguments.callee` in a strict function throws a TypeError.

explanation: Only sloppy functions with simple parameter lists get the "mapped" `arguments` object, whose indexes alias the parameters. Everything else gets a plain array-like copy. Modern code uses rest parameters (`...args`), which give a real array and work in arrow functions too.

options.text: `[0, 1, 2]`, because every iteration gets a fresh `i`
options.why: Each iteration has a fresh `i`, but `get` was created once, before the first copy was made.

options.text: `[3, 3, 3]`, because `get` sees the final value of `i`
options.why: The binding that `get` closes over is never incremented; the increments happen in the per-iteration copies.
`get` closes over the scope of the loop initialiser, whose `i` stays 0, while the loop runs on copies.

options.text: It throws a `ReferenceError`, because `i` is in the temporal dead zone when `get` is created
options.why: `i` is initialised to 0 before `get` is created, and `get` only reads it when called later.

explanation: The loop head creates a scope with `i = 0` and `get`, and `get` closes over that scope. Before the first iteration, the spec copies the bindings into a fresh per-iteration scope. The condition, body and `i++` all run in copies from then on. The original `i` that `get` sees is never changed, so every call returns 0.

`fn.length` counts only the parameters before the first default, so it is 1, not 3. `f(1)` already has 1 ≥ 1 arguments, so it calls `fn(1)` straight away: 1 + 10 (default) + 0 (the nullish fallback for `c`) = 11. Curry helpers that rely on `fn.length` quietly misbehave with default and rest parameters.

options.why: The hoisted function declaration makes `a` a local variable inside `b`.
Inside `b`, the function declaration `a` is hoisted, so `a = 10` overwrites the local `a`.
Shadowing happens only inside `b`; the global `a` is never touched and stays 1.

options.text: A function, because the declaration after `return` replaces the global `a`
options.why: Declarations are hoisted within their own function scope, even if they come after `return`.

explanation: Hoisting happens per scope and ignores control flow, so a declaration after `return` still counts. `function a() {}` creates a local `a` in `b`, initialised to that function. `a = 10` then reassigns the local, and the global `a` stays 1.

options.why: A plain method call sets `this` to `obj`.
Grouping parentheses keep the property reference, so it is still a method call.
Explicit binding sets `this` to `obj`.
An assignment expression evaluates to the bare function value, so `this` is `undefined`.
The comma operator also yields a bare value, losing the receiver.
This is a method call on the array, so `this` is the array, not `obj`.

explanation: A call sets `this` from the Reference it is made on. `obj.who` and `(obj.who)` are both property references with base `obj`. Assignment and comma expressions run GetValue and return the plain function, so the call has no receiver (`undefined` in strict mode). `[obj.who][0]()` is a property reference on the array.
